props.title: Geppetto
props.initialSlug: Toymaker's wish brings puppet son to life

sections.content: The 2000 made-for-TV adaptation of "Geppetto (2000)" offers an interesting musical spin on the classic Pinocchio (1940) tale, told from the perspective of the woodcarver father. Drew Carey takes on the titular role, bringing a mix of comedy and pathos that echoes the deeper themes of parenthood found in both Carlo Collodi's original story and Disney's animated masterpiece. While it doesn't reach the artistic heights of the 1940 animation, it joins other notable Pinocchio adaptations like Roberto Benigni's Pinocchio (2002) and Guillermo del Toro's stunning stop-motion Pinocchio (2022) in exploring the complex relationship between parent and child.

sections.content: The musical elements of "Geppetto" follow a tradition of reimagining classic children's stories through song, similar to other TV musical adaptations like Rogers & Hammerstein's Cinderella (1997) and Annie (1999). Stephen Schwartz, known for Godspell (1973) and later Wicked (2003) on Broadway, provides the soundtrack that helps illuminate Geppetto's internal struggles with parenthood. The songs, while not as memorable as the original Disney numbers, offer thoughtful perspectives on father-son relationships and the challenges of raising children.

The film's focus on Geppetto's journey predates a modern trend of retelling classic stories from different perspectives, as seen in films like Maleficent (2014) and Cruella (2021). This approach adds depth to what was previously a secondary character, exploring themes of loneliness, the desire for family, and the complexities of parental love that weren't fully developed in earlier versions. sections.content: "Geppetto" represents a specific moment in television's approach to family fantasy, bridging the gap between traditional adaptations and more modern retellings. It shares DNA with films like The Parent Trap (1998) and Mrs. Doubtfire (1993) in its exploration of parental devotion, while maintaining the magical elements that make the original story timeless. The production values, while modest by today's standards, exemplify the era's approach to family-friendly television movies.
